problem: Socially-aware navigation systems require experts to specify tasks and environment constraints via code or math formulas, task switching is unintuitive, and 2D laser scans miss hidden or 'potential' obstacles (e.g. spilled milk, carpets, areas around glass).
motivation: Home and public-space robots should understand user intent and environment details from natural interaction, without heavy visual recognition burden. Language alone cannot describe some spatial details, so hand-drawn sketches on a map can complement it, while an LLM handles task understanding.
key_idea: An LLM parses text/voice into task type, destination and constraint information using a semantic map and function library, sketches and constraints are merged into the laser map, and a single SAC RL policy executes point-to-point, following and guiding tasks.
insight: Injecting user-provided constraints (sketched or LLM-derived) into the laser map lets a single 2D-laser RL policy avoid undetectable hazards, and the ablation RL w/o CI fails mostly through safety-zone violations (75% and 82.5% failure rate type β) versus 22.5% and 12.5% for LIM2N. Multitasking is achieved by only changing the target g^t rather than training multiple models. RL lags human reflexes with unpredictable pedestrians, and manual control remains competitive in the pedestrian scenario.
method: LLM module: text or ASR-converted voice goes into an LLM backbone that picks the task type from a task pool and extracts destination info (goal, pedestrian ID, waypoints) and constraint info (obstacles, safety zones).

Semantic map + function library: a text-based map of building coordinates and sizes from 2D laser scans, plus functions such as expand_location(position, r) built on Numpy/Shapely, compensate for the LLM's lack of vision and computation. The LLM asks for clarification when instructions are ambiguous.

Intelligent sensing module / UI: users sketch on a map (closed shape = obstacle, line = route, extended outline = safe distance, click = goal). Sketches and LLM constraints are merged with live laser scans into a merged laser map. SPENCER pedestrian tracking gives position and velocity.

Task Mode Processing: sets the target g^t per task; point-to-point uses the end goal, following uses the VIP position, guiding first approaches the VIP then goes to the goal and returns to the VIP if the distance grows.
SAC policy: POMDP with continuous actions (v, w); observations are g^t and the merged laser map; reward covers goal reaching, collision, distance to goal and step penalty (following Yao et al. 2021).
Training: an OpenCV 2D simulator with fixed obstacles plus two random squares and four random line segments per iteration, and four simulated pedestrians driven by SFM and ORCA.

setting.backbone: LLM backbone (model unspecified, prompted) + SAC RL policy trained from scratch; SPENCER for pedestrian detection
setting.training_data: SAC trained in a custom OpenCV 2D simulator with randomized obstacles and SFM/ORCA pedestrians; LLM is used via prompting without training
setting.observation: 2D laser scan (RPLIDAR A1) merged with sketch/LLM constraints, plus camera used only for pedestrian detection
setting.privileged: pre-built semantic map and 2D laser map of the environment, user-provided sketches and constraints, pedestrian ID

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark. Success rates are only shown in figures (Fig. success_figure); Table 1 reports failure-rate types α/β/γ for MC w/ CI, RL w/o CI and LIM2N, not a standard metric. Not extracted as benchmark numbers.
results: In a static simulation scenario LIM2N had lower failure rates than RL w/o CI and manual control with constraint info (α 3.3%, γ 11.7% vs 20% and 18.3% for manual control). With pedestrians it was slightly behind manual control in success but lower α/γ (26.7%, 23.3%). A 15-participant user study showed LIM2N was stable with low variance in completion time and rated similar in intuitiveness to a joystick.
limitations: The RL policy struggles with unpredictable pedestrians and complex real-world dynamics due to the sim-to-real gap, and can trail human reflexes.
Relies on a pre-built semantic map and manual sketches; LLM model and prompts are not detailed; evaluation is small-scale and non-standard, with no comparison against other published methods.
Single-user only; multi-user handling and human feedback are left as future work.
builds_on: Kästner et al. 2022 (human-following and guiding navigation)
